name: Zhangzhung
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

tone_statements.citation: Stein, R. A. 1971. XII. La langue žaṅ-žuṅ du bon organisé. Bulletin de l'École française d'Extrême-Orient 58(1): 231-254. doi 10.3406/befeo.1971.5084
tone_statements.quote: 3. D'autres mots mu qui n'ont peut-être aucun rapport avec le précédent. Dans toute langue monosyllabique dont les tons ne sont pas marqués (comme en tibétain), il y a évidemment beaucoup d'homophones. On trouve : a) nam-mu « lieu » {gnas, 9, 5), mais aussi пат-lu (id., 15, 3) [...] On voit l'instabilité et l'incertitude qui régnent. Pour résumer, il me semble qu'à part des homophones inexpliqué», mu, dmu signifie essentiellement «ciel»
tone_statements.translation: 3. Other mu words that may have no connection with the preceding one. In any monosyllabic language whose tones are not marked (as in Tibetan), there are obviously many homophones. One finds: a) nam-mu 'place' (gnas, 9, 5), but also nam-lu (id., 15, 3) [...] One sees the instability and uncertainty that prevail. To sum up, it seems to me that, unexplained homophones apart, mu, dmu essentially means 'sky'.

sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent anywhere in the chapter. Sect. 5.1 gives the syllable canon (C1 C2 R V C3 C4) from the manuscripts; the only suprasegmental remark is p. 51: 'Is the language tonal or atonal? It is no doubt monosyllabic and includes many homophonic syllables; in other words, it is a typologically tone-prone type. Nevertheless, there is no sign to indicate the tonal contrasts.' Sect. 5.2 'Syllable Concatenation or Sandhi Phenomena': 'There is nothing much that can be said about this for the time being.'

sources.note: Only the Rosetta Project sample pages are open (contents; pp. 7-9; 12-13 'The orthography of the Zhang-zhung language' / 'phonetic range of the characters' / 'Finals'; sentence and numeral pages). The table of contents lists no stress/accent section, and pp. 12-13 discuss only letters, prefixes, subscripts and finals; nothing on stress. sources.citation: Martin, Dan (2010). Zhangzhung Dictionary. Revue d'Etudes Tibetaines 18: 5-336.
sources.note: Largest modern lexicon of Zhangzhung with an introduction; a text-based glossary, so a stress statement is improbable, but it is the fullest modern reference and was not reachable today.

Dans toute langue monosyllabique dont les tons ne sont pas marqués (comme en tibétain), il y a évidemment beaucoup d'homophones. sources.note: Stein's only remark on tone (p. 247) is an aside: he treats Zhangzhung as a monosyllabic language 'whose tones are not marked (as in Tibetan)' to account for the many homophonous mu/dmu words in the Bon-po bilingual texts; no tone inventory, no analysis, and nothing else on tone, pitch or accent anywhere in the 24 pages (the article is a philological study arguing much of the 'later' Zhangzhung vocabulary was fabricated on Tibetan models, with West-Himalayish comparisons of numerals etc.).
